title: The Top Sustainable Funds
text:
Leaders & Laggards—Fourth Quarter 2018
Most tellingly, Barron’s third annual survey of the funds in Morningstar’s database found that stockpickers who gravitated toward sustainable companies beat the broad market in 2018, just as they did in 2016 and 2017. Last year, 39% of the large-company funds on our list outpaced the large-cap S&P 500, versus 36% of all actively managed funds. In our previous ranking, 37% of our list’s members topped the market, compared with 28% of all actively run funds, according to Morningstar.
Topping our list are three funds that previously hadn’t cracked the top 25: Polen Growth (ticker: POLIX), Fidelity Focused Stock (FTQGX), and Calvert Equity (CSIEX). All of them have more than $2 billion in concentrated growth portfolios that returned over 5%, handily beating the S&P’s negative 4.4% total return in 2018.
ESG researcher and Morningstar partner Sustainalytics assigns a sustainability score to more than 10,000 companies worldwide, based on over 100 ESG factors. Morningstar then uses this information to assess the sustainability of each of the 35,500 funds in its database, based on the stocks they own. We used Morningstar data to screen for large-company U.S. stock funds with sustainability ratings of “high” (placing them in the 10th percentile of their category) or “above average” (top third).
In October, Morningstar altered the way it calculates a fund’s sustainability, and that is reflected in our ranking. Previously, a fund’s score was based on its holdings on a single day. Now, the ratings take into account 12 months’ worth of holdings, says Jon Hale, global head of sustainability research at Morningstar and creator of the rating system. The current portfolio snapshot is given more weight than those from prior months, which ultimately means that the sustainability rating won’t fluctuate as much. In other words: “It’s now more meaningful if a fund moves up or down a notch,” says Hale.
Barron’s looked for large-cap U.S. stock funds with assets of $300 million or more and at least one year’s worth of performance. That turned up 188 funds with more than $1 trillion in combined total assets. We ranked these funds by one-year returns for the 12 months ended on Dec. 31. In our previous ranking, 203 funds had met the same criteria; this year’s smaller list reflects asset shrinkage, thanks to market volatility and money leaving actively managed funds.
This list identifies market-beating funds with high sustainability ratings, and it will evolve as the tools to measure sustainability get sharper. Sustainalytics has overhauled how it scores companies, says the firm’s head of ESG research, Simon MacMahon. Companies are now scored on an absolute basis, instead of relative to others in its industry. Theoretically, this means that iPhone maker Apple (AAPL) could be compared with Orange (ORA.France), a European multinational telecom. Morningstar and Sustainalytics are in discussions for when that change will hit the portfolio ratings, says MacMahon.
As the metrics become more sophisticated, funds with truly sustainable portfolios will be easier to identify. There’s no such thing as being accidentally sustainable: Even when managers don’t hew to an explicit mandate, the best stockpickers seem to naturally look at the big picture, finding quality companies that are well-managed, with an eye toward long-term trends that can affect sustainability.
That’s arguably a better strategy than simply using ESG criteria as a check at the end of the stock-picking process, as some managers who claim to run sustainable portfolios seem to do. And some of the managers who already integrate environmental, social, and corporate governance considerations in their stock-selection routines are stepping up their analysis, in what John Streur, chief of Calvert Research and Management, a unit of Eaton Vance , dubs ESG 2.0.
“Five years ago, ESG research and engagement was focused on risk mitigation, finding companies that were struggling or had problems,” he observes. “That’s still an important function, but ESG 2.0 is about opportunity, identifying companies improving their competitive position. Few fund managers are doing that now.”
The top two funds on our list don’t have mandates to be sustainable, but have portfolios stuffed with companies that have high scores in that regard. And the funds’ high marks are encouraging their portfolio managers to be more thoughtful about their process.
The $2.5 billion Polen Growth fund, which tends to do well when the stock market is in turmoil, topped our list. Its manager, Dan Davidowitz, puts a premium on quality stocks, and what some might call “boring” issues— O’Reilly Automotive (ORLY), Adobe (ADBE), Mastercard (MA), and Microsoft (MSFT)—drove performance in the past year, he notes.
Davidowitz has started to read ESG analysis reports since he discovered that his portfolio received high marks for sustainability, and per the request of clients in Europe. The fund chief says the rating merely confirmed what he already knew. Some academic literature says companies that rank highly on ESG can outperform the market over long periods, but Davidowitz thinks about it differently. “ESG data showed us when you find world-class companies, they tend to be good corporate citizens, too. The causality is the other way around. Companies that do well tend to reinvest on doing the right things,” he says.
The $2.3 billion Fidelity Focused Stock fund finished in second place. That reflects solid stock-picking from veteran portfolio manager Stephen DuFour, who has been working at the Boston-based money manager for a little over a quarter-century. Stocks such as Adobe, Microsoft, Mastercard, and Boston Scientific (BSX)—again, ones that might be considered boring—boosted results in the past year. However, disruptive companies are what DuFour is after…but only at the right price.
Fidelity Focused returned 5% in the past year, outstripping 94% of its large-cap growth fund peers in that time. The portfolio manager has been studying up on why his stock-picking scores well on ESG after discovering that his portfolio had done well in our first annual ranking. “My job is to understand what variables are moving the fund in a positive or negative direction, so I put a team together to find what results in this and how we can augment it,” he says. “The early work identifies governance as a main factor, but we’ve got a lot more work to do.”
Places three through five in our rankings went to, in order, Calvert Equity, Brown Advisory Sustainable Growth (BAFWX), and John Hancock US Global Leaders Growth (USGLX).
Only four funds among our top 10 have a clear sustainability mandate: Calvert Equity, Brown Advisory, Jensen Quality Growth (JENSX), and Amana Growth (AMAGX). Amana is a Sharia-oriented religious fund, but the rest are concentrated growth vehicles that approach sustainable investing in differing ways.
Calvert’s ESG research analysts help guide portfolio managers in stock selection. Jensen uses environmental, social, and governance data primarily to vet companies, not to pick stocks, while Brown Advisory Sustainable Growth uses it to look for companies that will outlast others because of how they do business, such as prioritizing reducing carbon footprints and water usage, says David Powell, who co-manages the fund with Karina Funk. “We are playing offense with sustainability,” says Powell. That paid off. The fund had a market-beating 5% return in 2018.
Others that outperformed the market and scored well on sustainability include GMO Quality IV (GQEFX), MFS Massachusetts Investor Growth Stock (MIGFX), ClearBridge Large Cap Growth (SBLGX), and Vanguard PrimeCap (VPMCX). Newsletter Sign-up
The trio of Parnassus funds made our list for the third consecutive year.Parnassus Core Equity (PRBLX) landed in the top 30, but growth-oriented Parnassus (PARNX) sank from the middle of the pack to the bottom 25. And value-oriented Parnassus Endeavor(PARWX) fell to the bottom 10, after ranking No. 23 last year. All have consistently high sustainability ratings and excellent long-term investment records, but each will rise or fall as its investing style goes in or out of favor. “The market hasn’t acknowledged intrinsic value, at least our estimate of it, as money chased the highfliers, but that could change,” says Billy Hwan, who co-manages the Endeavor fund.
The $670 million Domini Impact Equity Investor (DSEFX) stayed near the bottom of the list, but its strategy is about to undergo some serious changes. For one, Domini decided to take over portfolio management duties for that particular fund from Wellington Capital Management, which still subadvises its other funds. Previously, Domini screened for its ESG standards, and Wellington constructed the portfolios from that list.
Now, the firm’s founder and chairman, Amy Domini, and its CEO, Carole Laible, are running the fund. They aim to turn Domini Impact into a broad core fund, rather than a concentrated portfolio. “We’re looking to deliver a product that classic responsible investors look for—exposure to the U.S. economy but in the better companies out there,” says Laible.
It remains to be seen whether the change will bolster performance. The fund has lagged behind the S&P 500 and more than 90% of large-blend peer funds over the past 15 years—exactly the kind of sustained performance that nobody wants. The Top Sustainable Mutual Funds Barron’s selected the top U.S. large-company, actively managed funds with the most sustainable portfolios, and ranked them by one-year returns. Of the funds, 39%, or the first 73 funds, beat the S&P 500 Index’s negative 4.4% return in the year ended on Dec. 31, 2018. Asterisks denote funds with a sustainable mandate–ESG-focused, socially responsible, or religious. The others come by their sustainable portfolios via their stock-picking process. The ranking was based on data provided by independent research firms Morningstar and Sustainalytics. Total returns as of Dec. 31, 2018; Three- and five-year returns are annualized; N/A=Not applicable; N/R=Not ranked
